text: This is it — the last lesson of Data Modeling & Data Warehousing. You've designed a real dimensional model and built it in T-SQL. This lesson isn't about adding anything else to it. It's about checking it against what you set out to build, and turning it into something you can actually show someone.

Look back at what got you here. Chapter 1 gave you the four-step business process modeling sequence this capstone just ran for real. Chapters 2 through 4 gave you fact table types, surrogate keys, and slowly changing dimensions — the exact vocabulary behind this design's accumulating snapshot fact table and its mix of Type 0, 1, and 2 dimensions. Chapters 5 through 7 gave you staging, advanced patterns like conformed dimensions, and the physical design, indexing, and partitioning decisions Lesson 38 put directly into practice.

When you show this off, order matters. Start with one plain sentence about the business process it models, not the implementation. Then walk through the grain and dimension list, and be ready to explain why the fact table is an accumulating snapshot instead of a plain transaction fact — that's a real test of whether you understand the design, not just the syntax. Save indexing and partitioning for last, and frame them honestly: that's the difference between a schema that's technically correct and one that would actually perform in production.

Keep the six CREATE TABLE scripts and a short README describing the scope table, and you've got a real, inspectable portfolio piece — not just a line on a resume. From here, this catalog's Microsoft Data & BI Capstone and Job Preparation course folds a project like this one into a full portfolio alongside your T-SQL, SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI work. Congratulations — you've designed and built a real dimensional warehouse, start to finish.
